Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We study the limiting eigenvalue distribution of $n\times n$ banded Toeplitz matrices as $n\to \infty$. From classical results of Schmidt-Spitzer and Hirschman it is known that the eigenvalues accumulate on a special curve in the complex plane and the normalized eigenvalue counting measure converges weakly to a measure on this curve as $n\to\infty$. In this paper, we characterize the limiting measure in terms of an equilibrium problem. The limiting measure is one component of the unique vector of measures that minimes an energy functional defined on admissible vectors of measures. In addition, we show that each of the other components is the limiting measure of the normalized counting measure on certain generalized eigenvalues.

outputs.L1: We study the limiting eigenvalue distribution of \(n\times n\) banded Toeplitz matrices as \(n\to\infty\). Classical results of Schmidt-Spitzer and Hirschman show that the eigenvalues accumulate on a distinguished curve in the complex plane, and that the normalized eigenvalue counting measure converges weakly to a measure supported on this curve as \(n\to\infty\). In this paper, we characterize this limiting measure in terms of an equilibrium problem. Specifically, the limiting measure is one component of the unique vector of measures that minimizes an energy functional over the class of admissible vectors of measures. In addition, we show that each of the remaining components arises as the limiting measure of the normalized counting measure associated with certain generalized eigenvalues.
outputs.L2: We investigate the asymptotic eigenvalue distribution of banded Toeplitz matrices of size \(n \times n\) in the limit \(n \to \infty\). Classical theorems due to Schmidt-Spitzer and Hirschman show that the eigenvalues cluster along a particular curve in the complex plane, and that the normalized eigenvalue counting measure converges weakly, as \(n\) grows, to a measure supported on this curve. In this work, we describe that limiting measure through an equilibrium problem. Specifically, it appears as one entry of the uniquely determined vector of measures that minimizes an energy functional over the class of admissible measure vectors. We also prove that every remaining component of this vector arises as the limiting normalized counting measure for certain generalized eigenvalues.

The study investigates the limiting eigenvalue distribution of \(n \times n\) banded Toeplitz matrices as the matrix size \(n\) tends to infinity. Such matrices have constant entries along each diagonal, with only finitely many nonzero diagonals. Because of this structured form, their spectral behavior exhibits a high degree of regularity in the large-\(n\) limit.

Classical results show that the eigenvalues of these banded Toeplitz matrices do not spread throughout the complex plane arbitrarily. Instead, as \(n \to \infty\), they accumulate on a distinguished curve in the complex plane determined by the Toeplitz symbol associated with the matrix. This curve captures the asymptotic location of the spectrum and plays a central role in describing the limiting spectral distribution.

More precisely, if one considers the normalized eigenvalue counting measure, which assigns mass \(1/n\) to each eigenvalue of the \(n \times n\) matrix, then this sequence of measures converges weakly to a limiting measure. The support of this limiting measure is contained in the special curve on which the eigenvalues accumulate. Thus, the asymptotic eigenvalue distribution can be understood as a probability measure supported on that spectral curve.

The paper provides a characterization of this limiting measure using an equilibrium problem from logarithmic potential theory. In this formulation, one considers a vector of measures and an associated energy functional involving both self-interaction and mutual interaction terms. The limiting eigenvalue measure appears as one component of the unique vector of measures that minimizes this energy functional under suitable constraints. This variational characterization gives a deeper potential-theoretic explanation of the limiting spectral distribution.

In addition, the paper shows that the remaining components of the minimizing vector of measures also have a natural spectral interpretation. They arise as limiting measures of normalized counting measures associated with certain generalized eigenvalues. These generalized eigenvalues are connected to auxiliary matrix problems derived from the original Toeplitz structure. Consequently, the entire vector equilibrium problem is not merely an abstract construction: each component of the vector measure corresponds to an asymptotic distribution of eigenvalue-like quantities associated with the underlying banded Toeplitz matrices.

The paper investigates the asymptotic spectral behavior of large banded Toeplitz matrices. Such matrices are determined by a finite number of diagonals, and their eigenvalues form structured sets in the complex plane whose limiting distribution, as the matrix size tends to infinity, has been studied in earlier work. The main object of interest is the limiting eigenvalue distribution, a probability measure describing how the eigenvalues of these Toeplitz matrices accumulate in the large-size limit.

A central result of the paper is a new characterization of this limiting measure through a vector equilibrium problem. In this formulation, one considers not just a single measure, but a vector of interacting measures supported on certain sets in the complex plane. These measures minimize a logarithmic energy functional that includes both self-interaction and mutual interaction terms. The paper proves that the known limiting eigenvalue distribution of the banded Toeplitz matrices appears as one component of the unique vector of measures solving this equilibrium problem.

In addition, the paper gives a spectral interpretation to the remaining components of the equilibrium vector. These other measures are shown to arise as limiting counting measures for generalized eigenvalues associated with related matrix pencils or auxiliary spectral problems. Thus, the vector equilibrium problem does not merely reproduce the known limiting eigenvalue distribution; it also reveals a broader spectral structure behind it.

Overall, the work connects the asymptotic eigenvalue theory of banded Toeplitz matrices with logarithmic potential theory and vector equilibrium problems. It extends the understanding of the limiting measure by embedding it into a larger variational framework and by identifying all components of the minimizing vector with natural limiting spectral distributions.
outputs.L5:
**From Toeplitz to Schmidt: Ideas in Linear Algebra and Analysis**

Toeplitz matrices and Schmidt decompositions are important concepts that appear in mathematics, physics, and engineering. Although they come from different areas, both are connected by the study of structure, symmetry, and efficient representation.

A **Toeplitz** matrix is a matrix in which each descending diagonal from left to right is constant. In other words, the value of an entry depends only on the difference between its row and column indices. Such matrices often arise in signal processing, time-series analysis, numerical methods, and operator theory. Their special structure makes them useful because large problems can sometimes be solved more efficiently than with general matrices.

**From** the perspective of applied mathematics, Toeplitz matrices are valuable because they model systems with translation-invariant behavior. For example, when a signal is filtered in the same way at every point in time, the resulting linear operation can often be represented using a Toeplitz matrix. This makes them closely related to convolution, Fourier analysis, and approximation theory.

The name **Schmidt** is often associated with the Schmidt decomposition, a fundamental tool in linear algebra and quantum mechanics. The Schmidt decomposition expresses a vector in a tensor product space as a sum of orthogonal terms. In quantum physics, it is especially useful for understanding entanglement between two systems. It reveals how strongly two parts of a system are connected and provides a simple way to analyze complex states.

Together, Toeplitz structures and Schmidt-type decompositions show how mathematics searches for hidden order. Toeplitz matrices simplify problems by exploiting repeated diagonal patterns, while Schmidt decompositions simplify high-dimensional objects by breaking them into meaningful components. From computational science to quantum theory, these ideas demonstrate the power of structure in understanding complex systems.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main results of a research article on eigenvalues of \(n\times n\) banded Toeplitz matrices as \(n\to\infty\), including the limiting measure and its relation to vector equilibrium problems.
counterfactuals.output:
For an \(n\times n\) banded Toeplitz matrix generated by a Laurent polynomial  

\[
A(z)=\sum_{j=-q}^{p} a_j z^j,\qquad a_{-q}a_p\neq 0,
\]

the matrix has entries constant along diagonals,

\[
T_n(A)=\bigl(a_{j-k}\bigr)_{j,k=1}^n ,
\]

with \(q\) nonzero lower diagonals and \(p\) nonzero upper diagonals. The main asymptotic problem is to describe the eigenvalues of \(T_n(A)\) as \(n\to\infty\).

The central results are as follows.

---

### 1. Limiting eigenvalue distribution

For each complex number \(\lambda\), consider the algebraic equation

\[
A(z)=\lambda .
\]

It has \(p+q\) roots, counted with multiplicity. Denote them by

\[
z_1(\lambda),\dots,z_{p+q}(\lambda),
\]

ordered so that

\[
|z_1(\lambda)|\leq |z_2(\lambda)|\leq \cdots \leq |z_{p+q}(\lambda)|.
\]

The limiting spectrum of \(T_n(A)\) is supported on the curve

\[
\Gamma_0=\left\{\lambda\in\mathbb C:\ |z_q(\lambda)|=|z_{q+1}(\lambda)|\right\}.
\]

This is the Schmidt–Spitzer curve. The normalized eigenvalue counting measures

\[
\nu_n=\frac1n\sum_{\lambda\in \operatorname{Spec}(T_n(A))}\delta_\lambda
\]

converge weakly to a probability measure \(\mu_0\) supported on \(\Gamma_0\):

\[
\nu_n \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} \mu_0 .
\]

Thus \(\mu_0\) is the limiting eigenvalue distribution of the banded Toeplitz matrices.

---

### 2. Explicit description of the limiting measure

The limiting measure \(\mu_0\) can be described in terms of the boundary values of the roots \(z_j(\lambda)\) on the two sides of the curve \(\Gamma_0\). In differential form, one has

\[
d\mu_0(\lambda)
=
\frac{1}{2\pi i}
\sum_{j=1}^{q}
\left(
\frac{z'_{j,-}(\lambda)}{z_{j,-}(\lambda)}
-
\frac{z'_{j,+}(\lambda)}{z_{j,+}(\lambda)}
\right)d\lambda ,
\]

where \(z_{j,+}\) and \(z_{j,-}\) denote boundary values from the two sides of \(\Gamma_0\).

This formula shows that \(\mu_0\) is obtained from the jump of the logarithmic derivative of the product of the \(q\) smallest roots of \(A(z)=\lambda\). The measure is positive and has total mass \(1\).

---

### 3. A hierarchy of spectral curves and measures

More generally, for each integer

\[
k=-q+1,\dots,p-1,
\]

define curves

\[
\Gamma_k
=
\left\{
\lambda\in\mathbb C:
|z_{q+k}(\lambda)|=|z_{q+k+1}(\lambda)|
\right\}.
\]

Associated with each \(\Gamma_k\) is a measure \(\mu_k\). The measure \(\mu_0\) is the limiting eigenvalue measure, while the other measures \(\mu_k\) arise naturally from the same algebraic equation and encode the interaction between different groups of roots.

The masses are

\[
\mu_k(\Gamma_k)=\frac{q+k}{q}.
\]

In particular,

\[
\mu_0(\Gamma_0)=1.
\]

---

### 4. Relation to vector equilibrium problems

A major result is that the family of measures

\[
(\mu_{-q+1},\dots,\mu_{p-1})
\]

is characterized as the unique minimizer of a vector equilibrium problem from logarithmic potential theory.

Roughly, one minimizes an energy functional of the form

\[
\sum_k I(\nu_k)
-
\sum_k I(\nu_k,\nu_{k+1}),
\]

where

\[
I(\nu)=\iint \log\frac1{|x-y|}\,d\nu(x)d\nu(y)
\]

is the logarithmic energy and

\[
I(\nu,\sigma)
=
\iint \log\frac1{|x-y|}\,d\nu(x)d\sigma(y)
\]

is the mutual energy. The measures \(\nu_k\) are constrained to live on the curves \(\Gamma_k\) and to have prescribed masses

\[
\nu_k(\Gamma_k)=\frac{q+k}{q}.
\]

The interaction matrix is tridiagonal: each measure repels itself logarithmically but attracts only its nearest neighbors. In equilibrium form, the measures satisfy relations of the type

\[
2U^{\mu_k}(\lambda)
=
U^{\mu_{k-1}}(\lambda)+U^{\mu_{k+1}}(\lambda)+\ell_k,
\qquad \lambda\in \Gamma_k,
\]

where

\[
U^\nu(\lambda)=\int \log\frac1{|\lambda-x|}\,d\nu(x)
\]

is the logarithmic potential and \(\ell_k\) are constants.

Thus the limiting eigenvalue measure \(\mu_0\) is not isolated: it is one component of a larger vector equilibrium configuration determined by the algebraic symbol \(A(z)\).

---

### 5. Main interpretation

The article shows that the asymptotic eigenvalue distribution of large banded Toeplitz matrices is governed by potential theory. The eigenvalues accumulate on algebraic curves determined by equality of moduli of consecutive roots of \(A(z)=\lambda\). The limiting measure on the principal curve \(\Gamma_0\) is the weak limit of the normalized eigenvalue counting measures. Moreover, this measure is part of a vector equilibrium problem whose solution is the full family of measures \(\mu_k\) on the curves \(\Gamma_k\).

In short:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Eigenvalues of }T_n(A)\text{ accumulate on }\Gamma_0,
\quad
\nu_n\to\mu_0,
\quad
\mu_0\text{ is part of a vector equilibrium problem.}
}
\]

counterfactuals.output:
We study the asymptotic spectral distribution of finite banded Toeplitz matrices
\[
T_n(a)=\bigl(a_{j-k}\bigr)_{j,k=1}^n,\qquad 
a(z)=\sum_{k=-p}^{q} a_k z^k ,
\]
through the geometry of the algebraic equation
\[
a(z)=\lambda .
\]
Let \(z_1(\lambda),\dots,z_{p+q}(\lambda)\) denote its roots ordered by modulus. The classical Schmidt–Spitzer theorem identifies the limiting eigenvalue set as the algebraic curve
\[
\Gamma=\{\lambda\in\mathbb C:\ |z_p(\lambda)|=|z_{p+1}(\lambda)|\},
\]
with refinements due to Hirschman describing the limiting eigenvalue counting measure on \(\Gamma\).

We formulate this limiting problem as a vector logarithmic equilibrium problem. To the branches \(z_j(\lambda)\) we associate a system of measures supported on the level-crossing curves
\[
\Gamma_k=\{\lambda:\ |z_k(\lambda)|=|z_{k+1}(\lambda)|\},
\]
and show that the limiting spectral measure is the first component, or an explicit linear combination of components, of the unique minimizer of a convex vector energy functional
\[
\mathcal E(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r)
=
\sum_{i,j} c_{ij} I(\mu_i,\mu_j)
+\sum_i \int V_i\,d\mu_i ,
\]
where \(I\) denotes logarithmic energy, the interaction matrix encodes nearest-neighbor coupling of the root moduli, and the external fields arise from the extreme powers of the Toeplitz symbol.

The Euler–Lagrange variational conditions for this equilibrium problem are shown to be equivalent to the analytic jump relations satisfied by the logarithmic potentials
\[
\log |z_j(\lambda)|.
\]
Consequently, the Schmidt–Spitzer/Hirschman accumulation curves appear as the supports of the equilibrium measures, while the Hirschman limiting density is recovered from the normal derivative jump of the associated equilibrium potential across \(\Gamma\).

This gives a potential-theoretic interpretation of the limiting spectrum of banded Toeplitz matrices: eigenvalue accumulation is governed not merely by the algebraic condition \(|z_p|=|z_{p+1}|\), but by a constrained vector equilibrium problem whose minimizer encodes both the spectral support and the limiting eigenvalue distribution.
